This module moves you from occasional AI use to a deliberate system. You learn the five parts every AI productivity system needs, how to break recurring work into steps and decide who does each step, and how to build the context store that makes an AI assistant genuinely useful for your work.

Most people use AI the way they use a calculator found on a table: when they remember it is there. They open a chatbot, type a quick question, copy the answer and move on. Next week they start again from nothing, explaining their organisation, their audience and their style all over again. The results are uneven, and the time saved is small and hard to see.

An **AI productivity system** is different. It is a small set of habits, files and checks that make AI part of how your recurring work gets done, every week, whether or not you feel inspired. The AI tool is only one piece. The system is what you build around it so that good results come out reliably and mistakes are caught before anyone else sees them.

What a system is not
**Not more apps.** A good system often uses fewer tools than before: one place to capture, one assistant, one home for files.
**Not automation without a human.** In this course every routine has a review gate. You decide what leaves your hands.
**Not AI everywhere.** Some tasks are faster done by hand, and some must never pass through an AI tool, such as private member records or money approvals.
**Not a one-day project.** You build it in small pieces and keep only what proves useful in your log.
Worked example: a coordinator's week before and after a system

For example, Ngozi coordinates volunteers for a women's network in Enugu. She has three weekly tasks and one monthly report. She timed each task for two weeks before building anything, then timed them again after setting up routines. All times include her checking and editing.
Monday announcement to the WhatsApp group: 40 minutes before, 15 minutes after (a saved prompt plus her context file gives a first draft she edits).
Answering repeat questions from members (venue, dues, dates): 60 minutes before, 30 minutes after (a facts sheet in her context store lets the AI draft replies she checks and sends).
Volunteer roster message: 30 minutes before, 12 minutes after (a template and a routine card).
Weekly total: 40 + 60 + 30 = 130 minutes before; 15 + 30 + 12 = 57 minutes after. She saves 73 minutes a week.
Monthly report: 180 minutes before, 90 minutes after. Over a four-week month she saves 73 x 4 = 292 minutes on weekly tasks plus 90 on the report, 382 minutes in all, a little over 6 hours.
Setup took her about 3 hours (180 minutes) spread over one weekend. At 73 minutes a week, 180 / 73 is about 2.5, so the weekly routines alone repaid the setup in under three weeks.
Ngozi gets back roughly six hours a month, and she can show the numbers because she timed the work before and after. Without the before figures, she would only have a feeling that things were faster.
Time it before you change it

Before you build any routine, time the task the old way at least twice. Use your phone's stopwatch and write the minutes in a note. Your own before-and-after figures are the only honest proof that the system works for you.
Why systems beat occasional use

Three things improve when AI use becomes a system. First, **quality becomes consistent**, because every run uses the same tested prompt and the same context, so you are not relying on how well you happened to phrase a question that day. Second, **checking becomes faster**, because you learn exactly where this routine tends to go wrong and you look there first. Third, **improvement compounds**: each time you fix a prompt or add a fact to your context store, every future run benefits.

The rest of this course builds each part in turn. In this module you map your work and build your context store. In Module 2 you choose tools, write routine cards and set up your review gate and log. In Module 3 you learn to help a team or a paying client build the same thing, and to present your own results as evidence.
Saved time is only real if quality holds

If a routine saves 20 minutes but sends out a wrong date that you then spend an hour correcting, it has cost you time. That is why the review gate and the log are part of the system, not optional extras.

The most common mistake in AI productivity is asking, "Can AI do this task?" The honest answer is usually "partly". A monthly report, a parents' update or a funding application is not one action. It is a chain of steps: gathering information, deciding what matters, writing, checking facts, formatting and sending. AI is strong at some of those steps and weak or risky at others. Systems are built at the level of **steps**, not whole tasks.

Step 1: a two-week recurring task inventory

For two ordinary weeks, keep a simple list of every task you do more than once a month. For each one, write how often it happens and roughly how many minutes it takes. Then multiply to get **minutes per month**. A 15-minute task done every working day (about 22 times a month) costs 330 minutes a month, far more than a 2-hour task done once a month. This simple multiplication often changes what you think your biggest time costs are.

Worked example: redesigning a monthly parents' update

For example, Amaka runs a tailoring training centre in Aba with 24 learners. Every month she sends each learner's parent or sponsor a short progress message on WhatsApp. She timed the task the old way and then redesigned it step by step.
Compile attendance from the paper register: 40 minutes. New role: Tool or template. She enters attendance in a sheet with a COUNTIF formula: 10 minutes.
Write a progress note per learner (skills learned, what to practise): 24 x 2 = 48 minutes. Role: Me only, because it needs her judgement. Still 48 minutes.

Write 24 personalised messages: 24 x 4 = 96 minutes. New role: AI drafts, I edit. She pastes her notes (first names only) in batches with a saved prompt: 20 minutes, plus 1 minute checking each message, 24 minutes. New total 44 minutes.
Add fee balances from her ledger: 20 minutes. Role: Me only. Balances are typed in by her after the draft and never pasted into the AI. Still 20 minutes.
Proofread and check tone: 15 minutes. New role: AI checks, I decide: 8 minutes.
Send on WhatsApp: 30 minutes. Role: Me only. Still 30 minutes.

Amaka saves 89 minutes a month, about 36 percent. Half of her steps did not change at all, and one of the biggest savings came from a spreadsheet formula, not from AI. That is a normal, healthy result.

An AI assistant knows a great deal about the world but nothing about you. It does not know your organisation's name, who your members are, which words your leader dislikes, or that your audience reads on small phones with costly data. If you leave that out, you get a generic answer and spend your time fixing it. If you supply it every time by typing, you waste time. The answer is a **context store**: written material you prepare once and reuse in every routine.

The short context file sits on top; the larger layers below are attached only when a routine needs them.
**Context file:** a short description of your role, organisation, audiences, tone, words to use or avoid, and preferred formats. It goes into every conversation.

**Examples:** two or three past outputs you were proud of. Showing the AI a good example is often more effective than describing one.
**Reference facts:** a dated facts sheet with correct names, titles, venues, dates, prices and programme details. Update it when anything changes, and write the date of the last update at the top.

Worked example: fitting a context file into 1,500 characters

For example, Halima is communications lead for a women's cooperative network in Kano and uses the free ChatGPT plan, where custom instructions allow up to 1,500 characters. Her first draft context file is too long. She counts characters in Google Docs using Tools, then Word count.
Her draft has six sections: role 310 characters, audiences 420, tone 380, words to avoid 260, formats 450, organisation history 520.
Total: 310 + 420 + 380 + 260 + 450 + 520 = 2,340 characters, which is 840 over the limit.
She moves the organisation history (520) out of the context file and into a reference document in a Project, because it is only needed for some tasks.
She shortens formats from 450 to 250 (minus 200) by keeping only her two most used formats, and audiences from 420 to 220 (minus 200) by cutting repeated description.
New total: 2,340 minus 520 minus 200 minus 200 = 1,420 characters, leaving 80 characters of spare room.

Halima's context file now fits the free limit and applies to every chat, while the longer history sits in a reference file used only when a routine needs it. Her first drafts now open with the network's correct name and tone without any extra typing.

What never goes into a context store

Keep out phone numbers, home addresses, health details, bank or BVN numbers, ID numbers, passwords and anything a member told you in confidence. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, gives people rights over their personal data, so use first names or roles in examples and keep personal records in your own protected files.
Keeping the store alive

A context store slowly goes stale: a venue changes, a programme is renamed, a new leader prefers a different greeting. Put a recurring reminder in your calendar for the first working day of each month to read your facts sheet and context file and update anything that has changed. Write the update date at the top. An out-of-date facts sheet is dangerous, because the AI will repeat old details with full confidence.

Comparing options with a weighted score

When you have two or three realistic options, do not choose by excitement. List what matters, give each criterion a weight that adds up to 100, score each option from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), multiply and add. The scores are your own judgements after trying each option for a few days.
Worked example: scoring three stack options

For example, Chioma runs a small events business in Port Harcourt from her phone. She tried three stacks for one week each and wrote her own scores. Weights: works well on her phone 30, data use 25, free plan covers her needs 20, easy to share with her assistant 15, privacy controls she understands 10.
Stack A (a chat assistant app plus her phone notes app) scored 5, 3, 4, 2, 4. Weighted: 150 + 75 + 80 + 30 + 40 = 375, so 3.75 out of 5.
Stack B (an assistant from the same company as the email and cloud documents she already uses) scored 4, 4, 4, 4, 3. Weighted: 120 + 100 + 80 + 60 + 30 = 390, so 3.90.
Stack C (a team workspace app with built-in AI) scored 3, 4, 3, 5, 4. Weighted: 90 + 100 + 60 + 75 + 40 = 365, so 3.65.
She checks the result against her gut feeling. Stack C shares best, but sharing only carries 15 points for a business of two people.

Stack B wins with 3.90, mainly because it shares easily with her assistant and keeps files where they already are. If Chioma hires more staff, the sharing weight would rise and Stack C might win, so she notes to re-score in six months.
Keeping data costs down
**Prefer text.** Typed chats use far less data than voice conversations, image generation or video.
**Upload big files on Wi-Fi.** Large PDFs and recordings for a Project or NotebookLM are best added when you have cheaper or free Wi-Fi access, not on mobile data.
**Make documents available offline.** Google Docs and Drive allow offline access on phones, so you can read and edit your context store and templates without data.
**Turn off auto-download** of media in WhatsApp for groups you only need to read.
**Batch your AI work.** Running three routines in one session uses less data and attention than opening the app ten times a day.

Worked example: a monthly savings group update

For example, Funmi is treasurer of a 30-member rotating savings group (ajo) in Ibadan. Each member contributes 5,000 naira a month. She keeps contributions in a Google Sheet and used to spend about an hour writing the monthly update.

Inputs: the sheet totals expected contributions with a formula: 30 x 5,000 = 150,000 naira. It shows 26 members paid in full (130,000 naira), 2 paid half (2 x 2,500 = 5,000 naira) and 2 have not paid.
Collected: 130,000 + 5,000 = 135,000 naira. Outstanding: 150,000 minus 135,000 = 15,000 naira (2 x 2,500 from the half payments plus 2 x 5,000 unpaid). She confirms the sheet shows the same figures.

Saved prompt: "Using my context file, write a warm WhatsApp update for our savings group. Collected this month: 135,000 naira of 150,000. Outstanding: 15,000 naira. Next meeting: [date from facts sheet]. Do not name anyone who owes. Under 120 words. Do not calculate or change any figure."
Check: she compares every figure and date in the draft with her sheet and facts sheet, and fixes one sentence where the draft said "most members" instead of "26 of 30 members".
Output: one group message, plus four short private reminders she writes herself to the members who owe, so nobody is shamed in the group.

The routine now takes Funmi about 20 minutes. The AI writes only the words; the sheet does the sums, and her check confirms every figure. Member names, phone numbers and amounts per person never enter the AI tool.
Tell the AI not to touch the figures

Add a line such as "Do not calculate or change any figure" to every prompt that includes numbers, and still check every figure yourself. Assistants sometimes round, reorder or recalculate numbers in a draft.
A research routine with source checks

Research is one of the most useful routines and one of the riskiest, because assistants can state wrong dates, amounts or eligibility rules confidently. The safe pattern is to **research from sources you have chosen**, ask for answers with citations, and then confirm every key fact on the official page yourself.
Trigger: first Monday of the month, 30-minute time box.
Inputs: links to official pages of the programmes you follow (government agencies, development partners, your funders), saved in a list in your files.
Add those pages as sources in a NotebookLM notebook, which answers with in-line citations to your sources, or paste the text into your assistant.

Saved prompt: "From these sources only, list each opportunity with: who can apply, deadline, how to apply. Quote the sentence each fact comes from. If a fact is not in the sources, write 'not stated'."
Check: open the official page for every deadline and eligibility rule and confirm it. Delete anything you cannot confirm.
Output: a short brief in your Drive and a summary message to your team, each with the official link.
Opportunity scams

Fake grant, loan and job offers often ask for an "application fee" or "processing fee" paid to a personal account. Treat any request for payment to access a grant as a warning sign, and confirm offers only through the organisation's official website or office.

A system that produces fast drafts but lets errors through is worse than no system, because people stop trusting your work. This lesson adds the two parts that keep the system honest: a **review gate** that catches problems before output leaves your hands, and an **AI work log** that shows, with your own figures, which routines are worth keeping.

Check in this order, because the first two catch the most damaging errors. Watch especially for **invented details**: an assistant may add a plausible venue, a speaker's title or a statistic that was never in your inputs. If a sentence contains a fact you did not supply, either confirm it from a reliable source or delete it.

Checking is fastest when you compare the draft with its sources side by side rather than reading it from top to bottom. On a phone, open the sheet or facts sheet in one app and the draft in another, then go through the draft looking only for names, dates and figures, ticking each one. Then read once more for tone. When a second reviewer is needed, send them the draft together with the sources and tell them what to look for, for example "please check the amounts against the attached sheet and confirm nothing private is included". A reviewer who knows what to check catches far more than one asked to "have a look".
The AI work log

Keep one line in a sheet for every routine run, with these columns: date, routine, minutes taken (including checking), estimated minutes without AI (from your before timings), edit level (none, light or heavy), and errors caught. It takes under a minute per run, and after a month it answers the question every manager and client will ask: does this actually help?

For example, Ngozi from Lesson 1.1 logged three weekly routines for four weeks: the Monday announcement (40 minutes before), repeat-question replies (60 minutes before) and the roster message (30 minutes before). That is 12 runs in all.
Announcement: 4 runs of 15 minutes = 60 minutes with AI, against 4 x 40 = 160 without. Saved 100 minutes, 25 per run.
Replies: runs of 30, 35, 25 and 30 = 120 minutes, against 4 x 60 = 240. Saved 120 minutes, 30 per run.
Roster: runs of 12, 14, 20 and 14 = 60 minutes, against 4 x 30 = 120. Saved 60 minutes, 15 per run.
Totals: 60 + 120 + 60 = 240 minutes with AI, 160 + 240 + 120 = 520 without. Saved 280 minutes, 4 hours 40 minutes.
Heavy edits: 3 of the 12 runs, which is 25 percent. Errors caught at the gate: 5 (two wrong dates, one wrong name, two invented details).

All three routines pass her keep rule. The five caught errors also show why the gate matters: without it, five mistakes would have reached members. The two wrong dates came from an old facts sheet, so her fix is to update the facts sheet, not the prompt.
A simple keep, fix or drop rule
**Keep** a routine that saves at least 10 minutes per run and needs heavy edits in no more than 1 run in 3.
**Fix** a routine that saves time but needs heavy edits often: improve the prompt, add an example or update the facts sheet, then log three more runs.
**Drop** a routine that still saves under 10 minutes per run after fixing, or that keeps producing errors. Doing the task by hand or with a plain template is a valid result.
Your fallback plan

Tools go down, data runs out and accounts get locked. A sound system keeps working at a slower pace. For each routine card, add a fallback line: where the offline template is, which past output you can adapt by hand, and the minimum version you will send if time is short. For example, "If no AI or no data: open last week's announcement offline, change dates from the facts sheet, send."
Monthly system review

On the first working day of each month, spend 20 minutes with your log: total the minutes saved, apply the keep, fix or drop rule, update your facts sheet and context file, and decide whether to add one new routine. One new routine a month is a sustainable pace.

When a team or small business asks for help "using AI", the request is usually vague. The owner has heard that AI saves time but cannot say where. If you jump straight to training on prompts, people try a few things, nothing sticks and the effort fades. **Discovery** is the short investigation you do first to find out how the work really flows, where time goes, and what the risks are. It turns a vague request into a short, specific plan.

Discovery starts with how the team actually works, not with the tools.

**Kickoff (Day 1, 45 minutes):** agree the goal, who takes part, what data you may and may not see, and the date of the findings meeting.
**Time diaries (Days 1 to 5):** each person notes recurring tasks and minutes spent, in a simple shared sheet or on paper. Keep it light: task name and minutes only.
**Role interviews (Days 3 to 4, 30 minutes each):** one conversation per role, ideally while they show you the task on their own phone or computer.
**Work samples (Day 5):** look at real reports, message threads and templates, with private details hidden, to see the current quality.
**Analysis (Day 6):** total the diary minutes, map tasks by frequency and judgement, and note risks.

Area

Ask to be shown, not told

People usually describe how a task should work. When they show you on their own device, you see the real version: the copying between apps, the searching through old chats, the workarounds. Those details are where routines save time.
Worked example: discovery at a small dispatch business
For example, Bisi is coaching a six-person delivery and dispatch business in Ibadan that works six days a week. After the discovery week she totals the time diaries.
Delivery status replies to customers on WhatsApp: 2 staff x 75 minutes a day x 6 days = 900 minutes a week.
End-of-day summary for the owner: 1 staff x 40 minutes x 6 days = 240 minutes a week.
Weekly payment reminders to business customers: 90 minutes a week.
Total: 900 + 240 + 90 = 1,230 minutes, which is 20.5 hours a week across these three tasks.

Risk notes: status replies contain customer names and addresses, so the routine must use saved reply templates and an AI-drafted FAQ rather than pasting customer details into a chatbot. The payment reminders involve money, so amounts come from the accounts sheet and the owner approves the wording once.

Bisi's findings shortlist three routines: a reviewed library of status reply templates drafted with AI, an end-of-day summary built from a shared sheet, and a payment reminder template with figures filled from the accounts sheet. Each has an expected saving to test, a named owner and a check.
Readiness and honesty

Discovery sometimes shows that AI is not the first fix. If the team has no shared sheet, uses five different WhatsApp groups for the same customers, or nobody knows the current prices, a simple template or a tidy-up will save more time than any AI routine. Say so plainly in your findings. Clients trust advisers who recommend the cheapest thing that works.

Present findings in a short meeting, not a long document. Show the diary totals first, because owners are often surprised by where the hours really go. Then show the three proposed routines, the risk and check for each, and what you will measure. End by asking the owner to choose a start date and name an owner for each routine. A findings meeting that ends without names and dates usually leads nowhere.
Handle discovery data with care

Time diaries and work samples can contain customer and staff details. Agree at kickoff what you will see, ask for private details to be hidden in samples, store notes in a protected folder, and delete copies you no longer need when the work ends.

Helping others build AI productivity systems can become paid work for a consultant or coach, or an internal service you offer as a team lead. Either way, clear scope and honest pricing protect both sides. The key fact about this work is that **habits take weeks to form**. Do not copy a rate from someone else's course or social media post without checking it against your local market.

Fee and payment: the costing table, contingency, total, payment dates and receipts.

If you lead a team inside an organisation rather than selling to clients, the same proposal still helps. Replace the fee with the staff hours you are asking for, and get your manager's written agreement on the scope and data rules before you start. Internal work without an agreed scope tends to grow until it stalls.
Terms that prevent later disputes
**The client owns the accounts.** AI tools, Drive folders and subscriptions are created in the client's name, so nothing breaks when you leave.
**Data rules in writing.** List what may go into AI tools (templates, anonymised examples) and what may not (customer details, staff records, payment information).
**Results are estimates.** Promise to measure, not a fixed number of hours saved. The log will show the real figure.
**Payment terms.** State amounts, dates and the account for payment, and issue a receipt for every payment.

Avoid promises like "double your productivity" or "save 20 hours a week". You do not yet know, and the client will remember. Offer to measure before and after, and let your log speak in the final review.

A personal system depends on one person. A team system must survive holidays, staff changes and busy seasons. That needs a shared, written **team AI playbook** and someone who leads adoption by example, not by announcement.
A person reviewing progress bars on a dashboard
Leading adoption means tracking whether routines actually run, week after week.
The team AI playbook
**Shared context file and facts sheet:** one version, with a named person responsible for updates and a date at the top.
**Prompt library:** tested prompts for each routine, numbered, with the date last tested.
**Routine cards with owners:** every routine has one named owner and one backup.
**Approved tools list:** which AI tools may be used for work, and with which accounts.
**AI use rules:** what never goes into AI tools, which outputs need a second reviewer, and how to label AI-assisted documents if your organisation requires it.
**Review rhythm:** a 20-minute monthly look at the log, owned by the team lead.
Champions, not commands

Pick one willing person per team as a routine champion. They run the routine visibly, help colleagues in the first weeks and report problems early. People adopt what they see a trusted colleague using successfully.
Handling worries and resistance

Some colleagues will be keen and some will hold back. Common worries are that AI will make mistakes in their name, that their job is at risk, or that they will look foolish while learning. Take each worry seriously. Point to the review gate: nothing leaves without a human check, and the person who sends it owns it. Explain that routines remove repetitive steps so people have more time for the work only they can do, such as customer relationships and judgement calls. Offer private practice time before anyone is expected to use a routine in front of others.

Watch the opposite risk too. Enthusiastic users sometimes skip the check because the drafts usually look right. A short monthly look at the log, including errors caught, keeps everyone honest without blaming anyone.
Measuring adoption

Time saved matters, but first you need to know whether routines are actually being run. The **run rate** is the number of routine runs completed divided by the number scheduled. A low run rate tells you the routine is too hard, poorly timed or not understood, and that problem must be fixed before measuring savings.
Worked example: six weeks of adoption at the dispatch business
For example, after Bisi's engagement the dispatch business ran three routines for six weeks, working six days a week.
Daily status replies drafted from the template library: scheduled 6 days x 6 weeks = 36 runs; completed 30.
Weekly summary report to the owner, built from the daily sheet: scheduled 6, completed 6.
Weekly payment reminders: scheduled 6, completed 4.
Total: 36 + 6 + 6 = 48 scheduled; 30 + 6 + 4 = 40 completed. Run rate: 40 / 48 = 83 percent.
The payment reminder routine is lowest at 4 of 6. In the review, staff explain it falls on Saturday, their busiest day. The owner moves the trigger to Thursday.

An 83 percent run rate shows the routines are mostly in use, and the one weak routine has a clear, simple fix. Bisi records the run rate, the minutes saved from the log and the change made as evidence for her portfolio, with the owner's permission.
An honest portfolio case study

Whether you want a promotion, a coaching client or a new job, evidence beats claims. One well-documented case is worth more than a list of tools you have used. Write it in five short parts, and include what did not work: it shows judgement and makes the rest believable.
**Starting point:** the task, who did it, and the before timings.
**What you built:** the context store, routine cards and checks, with a screenshot of one routine card (private details hidden).
**Measured result:** minutes saved from the log, run rate, errors caught at the gate.
**What did not work:** a routine you dropped or fixed, and why.
**What changed next:** the decision or improvement that followed.
Permission and privacy

Ask the client or your manager before naming them or sharing any figures from their work, and remove customer and staff details from screenshots. If they prefer, describe the case without the organisation's name, for example "a six-person dispatch business in Ibadan".

Why this matters
Occasional use versus a system
Stop starting from nothing every week
Build the five parts of a system
Decide who does each step: you, AI or a tool
Build a context store the AI can use

Most people use AI only when they remember it is there. They type a quick question, copy the answer, and next week they start again from nothing, explaining their organisation and style all over again.
A system is a small set of habits, files and checks around the AI tool, so good results come out every week and mistakes are caught before anyone else sees them.
The five parts
Every system has five parts
Capture: one place where everything lands
Context store: what the AI needs to know
Routines: repeatable steps with a fixed trigger
Review gate: check names, numbers, dates, tone
Log and improve: what each run cost and saved
First, capture. One notes app, or one WhatsApp chat with yourself, where ideas and requests land.
Second, a context store: what the AI needs to know about you and your work.
Third, routines. For example, every Monday at 8am, draft the weekly announcement.
Fourth, a review gate that checks output before it leaves your hands. And fifth, a log of what each routine cost and saved.
Tools change, but a written system moves to a new tool in an afternoon.
Worked example
Ngozi's week, before and after
Weekly tasks before: 130 minutes
Weekly tasks after, with checking: 57 minutes
Saved: 73 minutes a week
Setup: about 3 hours, repaid in under three weeks
Time the task the old way first, at least twice.
Ngozi coordinates volunteers for a women's network in Enugu. Before building anything, she timed her weekly announcement, member questions and roster message. Together they took 130 minutes.
After setting up routines, they took 57 minutes. That includes her checking and editing.
She saves 73 minutes a week. With her monthly report, that is a little over 6 hours a month.
Setup took about 3 hours over one weekend, so the routines paid for themselves in under three weeks.
Without the before figures, she would only have a feeling that things were faster. Use your phone's stopwatch and write the minutes down.
Steps, not tasks
Give every step one of four roles
Me only: judgement, money, private records
Tool or template: formulas and fixed layouts
Can AI do this task? The honest answer is usually partly. A task is a chain of steps, so write them in order and give each one a role.
Me only is for steps that need your judgement, approving money, or private member records.
AI drafts, I edit, means AI writes a first version and you correct and own it. AI checks, I decide, means you write and AI reviews.
And some steps need no AI at all. Chat assistants can make counting mistakes while sounding confident, so totals belong in a spreadsheet formula like SUM or COUNTIF.
Amaka redesigns her parents' update
Attendance: sheet with COUNTIF, 40 to 10 minutes
Progress notes: Me only, still 48 minutes
24 messages: AI drafts, she edits, 96 to 44
Fee balances: Me only, never pasted into AI
Total: 249 minutes down to 160
Amaka runs a tailoring centre in Aba with 24 learners. Each month she messages every parent. Attendance moved from a paper register to a sheet with a formula: 40 minutes became 10.
The progress notes need her judgement, so they stay hers.
For the 24 messages, AI drafts from her notes, using first names only, and she checks each one. 96 minutes became 44.
Fee balances she types in herself. They are never pasted into the AI.
She saves 89 minutes a month. Half her steps did not change, and one big saving came from a formula, not AI. That is a normal, healthy result.
Where to start
Which tasks get a routine first?
Routine first
Weekly announcements
Roster messages
Standard replies
Do it yourself
A letter to a funder
A disciplinary matter
Anything legal or financial
Start with tasks that repeat often and need little judgement. Each improvement pays back many times, and mistakes are easy to spot.
Rare tasks that need a lot of judgement stay in your own hands. And removing a task nobody reads saves more time than any routine.
Context store
Four layers of your context store
Context file: role, audiences, tone, words, formats
Templates: the shape of recurring outputs
Examples: two or three past outputs you liked
Reference facts: a dated facts sheet
An AI assistant knows nothing about you. So prepare a context store once and reuse it. A short context file, templates, good examples, and a dated facts sheet with correct names, venues and dates.

Check your tool's limits. On the free ChatGPT plan, custom instructions allow up to 1,500 characters. Halima's draft had 2,340, so she moved her organisation history into a project file and trimmed to 1,420.

What goes in, what stays out
Put in
Your role and audiences
Tone and words to avoid
Official programme names
Never invent figures, ask me

Phone numbers and addresses

Add a working rule: if information is missing, ask me rather than guessing.

Keep personal data out. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 gives people rights over their data, so use first names or roles. Keep a master copy outside the AI tool, and review your facts sheet monthly.

Why this matters
Fast drafts are not enough
Choose a lean, low-data tool stack
Set up your accounts safely
Write routine cards you can follow when tired
Catch errors and measure what you save
A system that produces fast drafts but lets errors through is worse than no system, because people stop trusting your work.
In this video you will choose your tools, turn tasks into routine cards, and add the checks and the log that keep the system honest.
Lean stack
One tool for each of four jobs
Capture: notes app or a chat with yourself
Assistant: one AI tool with your context
Home for files: one Drive or one folder
Calendar and reminders to fire routines
Every extra app is another password and more data used. So pick one tool for each job: one place to capture, and one assistant.
One home for files, and a calendar to fire each routine. Stay with your choice for at least a month before judging it.
To save data, prefer typed chats, upload big files on Wi-Fi, and make your documents available offline.
Safety first
Fraudsters sell fake AI apps and cheap shared logins on WhatsApp. Install apps only from the official store, pay only inside the official app or website, and never share your login or one-time codes.
Routine cards
A one-page recipe for one task
Trigger: a fixed time or event
Inputs: exactly what you gather first
Saved prompt: your tested wording
Check: what you verify before sending
Output and time box, then log the run
Prompts with numbers say: Do not calculate or change any figure.
A good intention fades within weeks. A routine card does not, because it answers every question in advance. When you are tired, you follow the card.
It says when the routine happens, what you gather, and which saved prompt you run.
Then what you check, where the result goes, and how many minutes you allow. The AI works only in the middle. You own the inputs, the check and the delivery.
Assistants sometimes round or recalculate numbers. So let a spreadsheet do the sums, tell the AI not to change any figure, and still check every figure yourself.
Worked example
Funmi's monthly savings group update
For example, Funmi is treasurer of a 30-member ajo in Ibadan.
Each member's monthly contribution
Expected this month
Collected
Outstanding
Totals come from her spreadsheet, not the AI.
Funmi used to spend about an hour on the monthly update. Now she follows a routine card.
Each member pays 5,000 naira, so her sheet's formula expects 150,000 naira.
The sheet shows 135,000 naira collected and 15,000 naira outstanding. Only these totals go into her saved prompt, with the words: do not name anyone who owes.
She checks every figure against her sheet, and changes most members to 26 of 30 members. Then she writes private reminders herself, so nobody is shamed in the group.
Member names, phone numbers and amounts per person never enter the AI tool. The routine now takes about 20 minutes.
Review gate
Match the check to the risk
Your own notes or a first list of ideas. A quick read for sense.
Messages to members or clients, reports, posts. The full five-point check.
Money, health, legal or official matters. Every claim sourced, plus a second reviewer.
Your own planning notes need only a quick read.

Messages to members, reports and posts get the full five-point check: names and dates, numbers, private data, sources, and does it sound like you. Watch for invented details, like a venue you never supplied.
Anything about money, health or legal matters needs every claim matched to a source and a second person to review it. Or do it without AI.
Work log
Ngozi reads four weeks of her log
520 minutes without AI, 240 with it
Saved: 280 minutes in four weeks
Heavy edits: 3 of 12 runs
Errors caught at the gate: 5
Keep it if it saves 10+ minutes a run, heavy edits at most 1 in 3.
Log one line for every run: date, routine, minutes, edit level and errors caught. Ngozi logged 12 runs over four weeks. They took 240 minutes, against 520 without AI. She saved 280 minutes.
Only 3 runs needed heavy edits, and her gate caught 5 errors, including two wrong dates. They came from an old facts sheet, so she fixed the facts sheet, not the prompt.
If a routine saves time but needs heavy edits often, fix it. If it still saves under 10 minutes after fixing, drop it. Doing a task by hand is a valid result.
Key points
Remember
One tool per job, set up safely
Routine cards: trigger, inputs, prompt, check, output
Sums come from the sheet, never the AI
Set the review gate by risk
Your own log decides keep, fix or drop

To remember. Keep your stack lean and secure. Write routine cards. Let the spreadsheet do the sums. Set your check by risk. And let your own log decide which routines stay. Every card also needs a fallback for days with no AI or no data.

Why this matters
Take your system beyond yourself
Find where a team's time really goes
Price a coaching engagement honestly
Lead adoption with a shared playbook
Present your results as a case study

When a team asks for help using AI, the request is usually vague. If you jump straight to prompt training, nothing sticks. So you start with discovery: a short investigation of how the work really flows.
Then you price the work, help the team adopt it, and turn the results into evidence for your portfolio.
Day 1: kickoff with the owner
Days 1 to 5: time diaries, task and minutes
Days 3 to 4: role interviews on their own device
Day 5: real work samples, private details hidden
Days 6 and 7: analyse, then a findings meeting
At kickoff, agree the goal, who takes part, and what data you may and may not see.
All week, each person keeps a light time diary: task name and minutes only.
In interviews, ask people to show you the task on their own phone. People describe how a task should work. When they show you, you see the copying between apps and the searching through old chats.
Then look at real samples, total the minutes, and present three first routines, each with its risk and its check.
Worked example
Bisi's discovery at a dispatch business
Status replies: 900 minutes a week
End-of-day summary: 240 minutes a week
Payment reminders: 90 minutes a week
Total: 1,230 minutes, 20.5 hours a week
Customer names and addresses never go into a chatbot.
Bisi coaches a six-person delivery business in Ibadan. Two staff spend 75 minutes a day, six days a week, answering customers about delivery status. That is 900 minutes a week.
The owner's daily summary takes 240 minutes a week, and payment reminders 90.
Together that is 20.5 hours a week. Owners are often surprised by where the hours really go.
Status replies contain customer names and addresses, so she uses saved reply templates instead. And payment amounts come from the accounts sheet, with the owner approving the wording.
Sometimes discovery shows a simple template or tidy-up is the first fix, not AI. Say so plainly.
Two offers
Build-and-coach
A workshop teaches ideas. It suits teams that only need the concepts.
But habits take weeks to form. A six-week build-and-coach engagement builds and tests routines with the team, and the log shows measured results.
Costing a six-week engagement
For example, Bisi prices the dispatch business engagement at 10,000 naira an hour.
33 hours at 10,000 an hour
With 15% contingency, rounded
50% paid on signing
Illustrative rate for practice, not a market rate.
Bisi estimates hours for each stage: discovery, building the routines, training, six weekly check-ins, and the final review. That adds up to 33 hours.
33 hours at an illustrative 10,000 naira is 330,000 naira.
She adds 15% contingency for things taking longer, and rounds to 380,000 naira.
Half, 190,000 naira, is paid on signing and half on handover, with a receipt for every payment.
If the owner wants a lower price, she removes a stage instead of cutting her rate. And she never promises a fixed number of hours saved. She promises to measure.
Team adoption
Shared context file and dated facts sheet
Prompt library, with date last tested
Routine cards, each with an owner and a backup
Approved tools list
AI use rules: what never goes in, who reviews
A 20-minute monthly look at the log
A team system must survive holidays and staff changes, so write it down in a shared playbook.

Pick one willing person as a routine champion. People adopt what they see a trusted colleague using. And when someone worries that AI will make mistakes in their name, point to the review gate: nothing leaves without a human check.
Measure adoption
Is the team really running the routines?
Run rate = completed runs / scheduled runs
Six weeks: 40 of 48 runs completed
Run rate: 83 percent
Payment reminders: only 4 of 6
Fix: move the trigger from Saturday to Thursday
Before measuring time saved, check that routines are actually being run.
Over six weeks, the dispatch business completed 40 of 48 scheduled runs. That is 83 percent.
Payment reminders were weakest. Staff explained they fell on Saturday, their busiest day. So the owner moved them to Thursday. A low run rate usually has a simple fix.
Your portfolio
An honest case study in five parts
Starting point and before timings
What you built, with one routine card
Measured result: minutes, run rate, errors
What did not work, and why
What changed next
Evidence beats claims. Show where you started, what you built, and what your log measured.
Include what did not work. It shows judgement and makes the rest believable.
Ask permission before naming a client or sharing their figures, and hide customer details in screenshots.
Key points
Remember
Discovery first: diaries, interviews, real samples
Cost by stage, plus 10 to 20 percent contingency
The client owns the accounts; data rules in writing
Fix a low run rate before measuring savings
Case studies include what did not work

To remember. Start with discovery. Cost by stage, with contingency. Keep accounts in the client's name and data rules in writing. Check the run rate first. And tell the whole story in your case study.
